[LLM] Algernon web server spawning shell child process (CVE-2026-45721 handler.lua RCE) Exploitation High
Detects the Algernon web server binary spawning /bin/sh, /bin/bash or cmd.exe — the exact primitive used by handler.lua's run3() / os.execute() / io.popen() when the parent-directory traversal bug loads attacker-controlled Lua. Algernon's normal request handling does not fork shells; this pattern is the live exploitation signature. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit exploitation primitive: run3() at engine/basic.go:142 calls exec.Command("sh", "-c", ...) via lua/run3/run3.go:23, plus the unsandboxed gopher-lua os.execute / io.popen exposed because lua/pool/pool.go:34 omits SkipOpenLibs. The parent-process pivot (algernon) plus a shell child is article-specific and not covered by generic 'web server spawns shell' rules without the algernon binary name. Cross-checked GitHub xyproto/algernon repository structure to confirm 'algernon' is the canonical binary name; no external NVD entry yet (fresh GHSA-xwcr-wm99-g9jc). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/xyproto/algernon • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xwcr-wm99-g9jc
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
// CVE-2026-45721 — Algernon parent process spawning a shell. Stock Algernon never forks /bin/sh for request handling; this is the run3()/os.execute() primitive that handler.lua exposes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "algernon"
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/algernon"
   or InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^algernon(\.exe)?$"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ash","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
// classic exploit shape: sh -c <attacker payload> launched by web server
| extend ShellArgs = iff(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-c ","/c ","-Command","-EncodedCommand"), "shell-with-inline-cmd", "interactive-or-script")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          ShellArgs, SHA256, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc
// CVE-2026-45721 — Algernon spawning shell on the ASIM cross-vendor process schema. Catches Linux (auditd) + Windows (4688/Sysmon) feeds.
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(^|/)algernon(\.exe)?$"
| where TargetProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(^|/)(sh|bash|dash|zsh|ash|cmd\.exe|powershell\.exe|pwsh\.exe)$"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| extend ShellWithInlineCmd = iff(TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("-c ","/c ","-Command","-EncodedCommand"), true, false)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildName = TargetProcessName,
          ChildCmd  = TargetProcessCommandLine,
          ShellWithInlineCmd, EventVendor, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] handler.lua dropped outside Algernon's configured web root (CVE-2026-45721 backdoor stage) Installation High
Algernon's vulnerable DirPage walks UP from the requested directory looking for handler.lua and executes the first match with full Lua/run3/httpclient privileges. This rule alerts on any process writing a file named handler.lua into a parent-of-webroot location (/, /srv, /var, /home, /tmp, /dev/shm) — the staging artefact that turns the bug into pre-auth RCE. Rationale: The article enumerates the exact candidate paths the vulnerable DirPage loop probes for each canonical Algernon invocation (/srv/handler.lua, /var/www/handler.lua, /home/<user>/handler.lua, /handler.lua, plus the /dev/shm extraction-dir variant from engine/handlers.go:249-266). A file write of handler.lua into ANY of those paths is the persistence artefact the bug weaponises — high specificity because legitimate Algernon deployments place handler.lua INSIDE the served tree (e.g. /srv/site/handler.lua), not in /srv/ or /var/. Cross-checked xyproto/algernon samples/ tree which confirms handler.lua only lives inside per-app subdirectories under samples/, never at samples/ root. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/xyproto/algernon • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xwcr-wm99-g9jc
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1547 T1574
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
// CVE-2026-45721 — handler.lua written into a parent of any plausible Algernon web root. The article's exploit places it at /srv/handler.lua, /var/handler.lua, /home/<user>/handler.lua, /dev/shm/handler.lua, or filesystem root.
let WebRootAncestors = dynamic([
    "/handler.lua",
    "/srv/handler.lua",
    "/var/handler.lua",
    "/var/www/handler.lua",
    "/home/handler.lua",
    "/tmp/handler.lua",
    "/dev/shm/handler.lua",
    "/opt/handler.lua",
    "/usr/local/handler.lua",
    "/run/handler.lua"
]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FileName =~ "handler.lua"
| extend FullPath = strcat(FolderPath, iff(FolderPath endswith "/" or FolderPath endswith "\\", "", "/"), FileName)
| where FullPath in~ (WebRootAncestors)
   or FolderPath matches regex @"^/home/[^/]+/?$"
   or FolderPath matches regex @"^/srv/?$"
   or FolderPath matches regex @"^/var(/www)?/?$"
   or FolderPath in~ ("/","/tmp","/dev/shm","/run","/opt","/usr/local")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
// .alg archive extraction by algernon itself is a documented vector — keep but tag it
| extend ExtractedByAlgernon = iff(InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "algernon", true, false)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FullPath, FolderPath,
          WriterImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          WriterCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          WriterUser  = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          ExtractedByAlgernon, SHA256, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc
// CVE-2026-45721 — handler.lua dropped into a parent-of-webroot path. ASIM ImFileEvent covers Linux (auditd) + Windows (Sysmon EID 11) feeds.
let WebRootAncestors = dynamic([
    "/handler.lua",
    "/srv/handler.lua",
    "/var/handler.lua",
    "/var/www/handler.lua",
    "/home/handler.lua",
    "/tmp/handler.lua",
    "/dev/shm/handler.lua",
    "/opt/handler.lua",
    "/usr/local/handler.lua",
    "/run/handler.lua"
]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName =~ "handler.lua"
| where TargetFilePath in~ (WebRootAncestors)
   or TargetFilePath matches regex @"^/home/[^/]+/handler\.lua$"
   or TargetFilePath matches regex @"^/var(/www)?/handler\.lua$"
| extend ExtractedByAlgernon = iff(ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(^|/)algernon$", true, false)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath,
          WriterCmd  = ActingProcessCommandLine,
          WriterName = ActingProcessName,
          WriterUser = ActorUsername,
          ExtractedByAlgernon, EventVendor, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Algernon vulnerable installation discovery (CVE-2026-45721 exposure inventory) Reconnaissance High
Hunts every host where the Algernon Go web server is installed or running so the SOC can map the blast radius of CVE-2026-45721. The bug is unauthenticated and applies to all currently-published versions until a patched release ships; identifying every algernon instance is a prerequisite to applying compensating controls (chmod 700 on parent dirs, blocking inbound traffic, or scheduled patching). Rationale: The article makes clear the bug is reachable on a stock unauth GET / against any Algernon install regardless of configuration, so the population that needs hunting is 'every host running algernon'. Two pivots — TVM software inventory and runtime ProcessRollup2/ImProcessCreate — cover both managed (TVM-onboarded) and unmanaged Linux/Windows boxes. Pulled the runtime command line so analysts can immediately read the configured --prod / web-root flag and reason about which ancestor paths are reachable. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/xyproto/algernon • https://github.com/xyproto/algernon/releases • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xwcr-wm99-g9jc
ATT&CKT1190 T1592.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
// CVE-2026-45721 — discover every host with Algernon installed or running. Two pivots: TVM inventory (slower, accurate) + recent process executions (faster, covers running instances).
let TvmHits =
    DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
    | where SoftwareName has "algernon" or SoftwareVendor =~ "xyproto"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, Source="TVM";
let ProcessHits =
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "algernon" or FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)(^|/)algernon(\.exe)?$"
    | summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp),
                CmdLines=make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 20),
                ParentBins=make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 10),
                RunAsUsers=make_set(AccountName, 10)
                by DeviceId, DeviceName, FileName, SHA256
    | extend Timestamp=LastSeen, OSPlatform="unknown", SoftwareVendor="xyproto", SoftwareName="algernon", SoftwareVersion=tostring(SHA256), Source="ProcessExec"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, Source, FirstSeen, LastSeen, CmdLines, ParentBins, RunAsUsers;
union isfuzzy=true TvmHits, ProcessHits
| order by DeviceName asc, Timestamp desc
// CVE-2026-45721 — Sentinel exposure inventory. DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory is not in standard Sentinel; pivot via DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities (if XDR connector is on) plus ASIM ImProcessCreate for runtime evidence.
let TvmHits =
    DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
    | where SoftwareName has "algernon" or SoftwareVendor =~ "xyproto" or CveId =~ "CVE-2026-45721"
    | project TimeGenerated, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, Source="TVM";
let ProcessHits =
    ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(^|/)algernon(\.exe)?$"
       or TargetProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(^|/)algernon(\.exe)?$"
    | extend AlgernonPath = iff(TargetProcessName matches regex @"(?i)algernon", TargetProcessName, ActingProcessName)
    | extend AlgernonCmd  = iff(TargetProcessName matches regex @"(?i)algernon", TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine)
    | summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated),
                CmdLines=make_set(AlgernonCmd, 20),
                RunAsUsers=make_set(ActorUsername, 10)
                by DvcHostname, AlgernonPath
    | extend TimeGenerated=LastSeen, SoftwareVendor="xyproto", SoftwareName="algernon", CveId="CVE-2026-45721", Source="ProcessExec"
    | project TimeGenerated, DeviceName=DvcHostname, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, AlgernonPath, CveId, Source, FirstSeen, LastSeen, CmdLines, RunAsUsers;
union isfuzzy=true TvmHits, ProcessHits
| order by DeviceName asc, TimeGenerated desc
(source:linux.auditd OR source:windows.sysmon OR source:windows.security) (@process.executable.path:(*/algernon OR *\\algernon.exe) OR @Image:(*\\algernon.exe OR *\\Algernon.exe) OR @process.name:algernon OR @process.command_line:*algernon*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/(\/|\\)algernon(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName], function={ count(), min(@timestamp), max(@timestamp), collect([CommandLine, UserName, SHA256HashData]) })
ENDPOINT

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45721")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

[LLM] npm install of compromised @opensearch-project/opensearch versions 3.5.3/3.6.2/3.7.0/3.8.0 Delivery High
Hunts for Node.js / npm process executions that resolve, fetch, or install the four malicious tagged versions published in the 12-May-2026 force-push CI compromise. Tightest possible install-time signal — fires on the exact package@version string the advisory enumerates. Rationale: Anchors on the four exact malicious versions enumerated in the advisory and the canonical Node toolchain binaries that resolve them. Highlighting the 00:00Z-10:00Z 2026-05-12 window via InWindow distinguishes guaranteed-compromised installs from later catalogue references. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/TanStack/router/security/advisories/GHSA-g7cv-rxg3-hmpx
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe")
   or FileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "@opensearch-project/opensearch"
     or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "@opensearch-project/opensearch"
| extend MaliciousVersion = case(
    ProcessCommandLine has "@opensearch-project/opensearch@3.5.3" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "@opensearch-project/opensearch@3.5.3", "3.5.3",
    ProcessCommandLine has "@opensearch-project/opensearch@3.6.2" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "@opensearch-project/opensearch@3.6.2", "3.6.2",
    ProcessCommandLine has "@opensearch-project/opensearch@3.7.0" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "@opensearch-project/opensearch@3.7.0", "3.7.0",
    ProcessCommandLine has "@opensearch-project/opensearch@3.8.0" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "@opensearch-project/opensearch@3.8.0", "3.8.0",
    "unknown-version-of-affected-pkg")
| extend InWindow = Timestamp between (datetime(2026-05-12T00:00:00Z) .. datetime(2026-05-12T10:00:00Z))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InWindow, MaliciousVersion, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","\\yarn.exe","\\pnpm.exe","\\npx.exe") or ParentProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","\\yarn.exe","\\pnpm.exe"))
| where CommandLine has "@opensearch-project/opensearch"
| extend MaliciousVersion = case(
    CommandLine has "@opensearch-project/opensearch@3.5.3", "3.5.3",
    CommandLine has "@opensearch-project/opensearch@3.6.2", "3.6.2",
    CommandLine has "@opensearch-project/opensearch@3.7.0", "3.7.0",
    CommandLine has "@opensearch-project/opensearch@3.8.0", "3.8.0",
    "unknown-version-of-affected-pkg")
| extend InWindow = TimeGenerated between (datetime(2026-05-12T00:00:00Z) .. datetime(2026-05-12T10:00:00Z))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, SubjectUserName, InWindow, MaliciousVersion, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] On-disk presence of malicious @opensearch-project/opensearch payload SHA256 Installation High
Hunts for write or open of any file whose SHA256 matches one of the three malicious artefacts shipped with the four compromised versions. Hash-based pivot catches the payload even if the package was renamed, vendored, or unzipped from a tarball off-line. Rationale: Uses the three SHA256 IOCs the GHSA enumerates — single-source on advisory but hash matches are zero-FP by construction. Pivot via DeviceFileEvents/ImFileEvent rather than IOC threat-feed correlation so it fires even when the package is unpacked from a tarball or copied from a private mirror. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/TanStack/router/security/advisories/GHSA-g7cv-rxg3-hmpx

[LLM] Mini Shai-Hulud / TeamPCP C2 beacon to api.masscan.cloud / git-tanstack.com / *.getsession.org Command & Control High
Detects outbound DNS or HTTP requests to the four C2 / data-exfil domains hard-coded in the compromised @opensearch-project/opensearch payload. Catches the post-install beacon even when host telemetry of the install itself was missed. Rationale: Pivots on the four article-named domains across DNS, proxy/firewall (CommonSecurityLog), ASIM DNS/web, and EDR. Sigma is skipped because the union across DNS+proxy+ASIM+web tables can't be expressed in single-event-shape Sigma. Sentinel query uses each table's actual hostname/IP columns (Computer/ClientIP on DnsEvents, DvcHostname/SrcIpAddr on ImDnsActivity, SourceHostName/SourceIP on CommonSecurityLog). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/TanStack/router/security/advisories/GHSA-g7cv-rxg3-hmpx • https://github.com/TanStack/router/issues/7383
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

| where RemoteUrl has_any (BadDomains)
     or tostring(parse_url(RemoteUrl).Host) in~ (BadDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
let BadDomains = dynamic(["api.masscan.cloud","git-tanstack.com","filev2.getsession.org","seed1.getsession.org"]);
let DnsHits = DnsEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Name has_any (BadDomains)
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = Computer, ClientAddr = ClientIP, Domain = Name, Source = "DnsEvents";
let AsimDnsHits = ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DnsQuery has_any (BadDomains)
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = DvcHostname, ClientAddr = SrcIpAddr, Domain = DnsQuery, Source = strcat("ImDnsActivity:", EventProduct);
let CslHits = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DestinationDnsDomain has_any (BadDomains)
        or DestinationHostName has_any (BadDomains)
        or RequestURL has_any (BadDomains)
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = SourceHostName, ClientAddr = SourceIP, Domain = coalesce(DestinationDnsDomain, DestinationHostName, RequestURL), Source = strcat("CommonSecurityLog:", DeviceVendor, ":", DeviceProduct);
let WebHits = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Url has_any (BadDomains) or HttpHostName has_any (BadDomains) or DstHostname has_any (BadDomains)
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = SrcHostname, ClientAddr = SrcIpAddr, Domain = coalesce(HttpHostName, DstHostname, Url), Source = strcat("ImWebSession:", EventProduct);
union isfuzzy=true DnsHits, AsimDnsHits, CslHits, WebHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Postinstall script execution from compromised @opensearch-project/opensearch package Installation Medium
Detects node child processes whose ancestor is npm/yarn/pnpm running an install/ci on the affected package — the malicious payload is delivered via a postinstall lifecycle hook that spawns shell/node/curl. Catches the active-execution moment regardless of whether the version string was logged at install time. Rationale: Targets the postinstall-hook spawn pattern that the Shai-Hulud / TanStack-router compromise pattern relies on — node/npm parent + script-host/curl child while the package path is in scope. Parent CommandLine carries the package name even when the version string isn't logged. Tagged hunting because legitimate postinstall hooks (esbuild, sharp, sqlite3) generate similar shapes — pair with UC1/UC2 for high-confidence triage. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/TanStack/router/security/advisories/GHSA-g7cv-rxg3-hmpx
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1546 T1195.002

     or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "node_modules\\@opensearch-project\\opensearch"
     or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "node_modules/@opensearch-project/opensearch")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","node.exe")
     or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Invoke-WebRequest","DownloadString","curl ","wget ","Buffer.from","child_process","eval(","http.get","https.request")

id: 9f0b4d12-8e3a-4ce1-bf12-2c0e1a5f6d7e
description: Detects npm/yarn/pnpm/node spawning a script-host or download utility while installing the GHSA-27f5-xjrr-q9ff @opensearch-project/opensearch package - characteristic of the malicious postinstall lifecycle hook.
references:

logsource:

detection:
    parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\node.exe'
            - '\npm.exe'
            - '\yarn.exe'
            - '\pnpm.exe'
            - '\npx.exe'
        ParentCommandLine|contains:
            - '@opensearch-project/opensearch'
    child_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\curl.exe'
            - '\wget.exe'
            - '\certutil.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
            - '\bash.exe'
            - '\sh.exe'
    child_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'Invoke-WebRequest'
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Buffer.from'
            - 'child_process'
            - 'eval('
    condition: parent and (child_image or child_cmd)
level: high

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/^(node|npm|yarn|pnpm|npx)\.exe$/i OR regex("/(node|npm|yarn|pnpm|npx)$", field=ParentImageFileName)
| regex("@opensearch-project/opensearch|node_modules[\\\\/]@opensearch-project[\\\\/]opensearch", field=ParentCommandLine)
| (ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh|cmd|curl|wget|certutil|bitsadmin|bash|sh)\.exe$/i OR regex("(Invoke-WebRequest|DownloadString|Buffer\\.from|child_process|eval\\()", field=CommandLine))

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The New Phishing Click: How OAuth Consent Bypasses MFA

The Hacker News
2026-05-19 14 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

In February 2026, a phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) platform called EvilTokens went live. Within five weeks, it had compromised more than 340 Microsoft 365 organizations across five countries.&nbsp; The targets of the platform received a message asking them to enter a short code at microsoft.com/devicelogin and complete their normal MFA challenge, then walked away believing they had verified a

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Microsoft Entra device code authentication flow used for sign-in (EvilTokens consent-phish entry vector) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] New OAuth consent grant for Mail/Files/Calendar/Contacts scopes (consent phishin · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Non-interactive OAuth refresh token sign-in from previously unseen IP / country
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] User granting consent to 3+ new OAuth applications within a short window (toxic combination) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
[LLM] Microsoft Entra device code authentication flow used for sign-in (EvilTokens consent-phish entry vector) Delivery High
Hunts the EvilTokens primary lure: victims enter a short code at microsoft.com/devicelogin and complete legitimate MFA, handing the operator a refresh token. The OAuth2 device-code grant flow is rarely needed by knowledge workers and is the signature first-stage telemetry for this PhaaS campaign. Rationale: Article explicitly names microsoft.com/devicelogin as the EvilTokens lure URL — that endpoint is exclusively the OAuth2 device-code grant flow. Detecting non-zero device-code authentications in a tenant where users normally sign in via browser/SSO is the cleanest pivot. Cross-checked Microsoft documentation on AuthenticationProtocol=deviceCode and Volexity/Mandiant prior writeups on identical Storm-2372 device-code-phishing TTPs. Cross-checked against: • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/monitoring-health/concept-sign-ins • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2025/02/13/multiple-russian-threat-actors-targeting-microsoft-device-code-authentication/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1528
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| extend ProcessingDetailsStr = tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails)
| where ProcessingDetailsStr has "deviceCode" or ProcessingDetailsStr has "Device Code" or ProcessingDetailsStr has "device_code"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Country, City, Application, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, IsInteractive, UserAgent, ProcessingDetailsStr
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == 0
| extend ProcDetails = tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails), AuthDetails = tostring(AuthenticationDetails)
| where ProcDetails has "deviceCode" or ProcDetails has "Device Code" or AuthDetails has "deviceCode"
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, Location, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, IsInteractive, UserAgent, ProcDetails
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Microsoft Entra Device Code Authentication Flow (Consent Phishing Indicator)
id: 0a1b2c3d-4e5f-6789-abcd-ef0123456789
description: Detects sign-ins using the OAuth2 device-code grant flow, the primary vector used by EvilTokens PhaaS to obtain refresh tokens scoped to Mail/Files/Calendar/Contacts without tripping MFA.

| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where firstTime > relative_time(now(), "-7d")
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.signature_id="deviceCode" OR Authentication.authentication_method="deviceCode" OR Authentication.signature="*deviceCode*" by Authentication.user Authentication.src Authentication.app Authentication.dest

[LLM] New OAuth consent grant for Mail/Files/Calendar/Contacts scopes (consent phishin Installation High
Hunts the EvilTokens payoff event: a user clicks Accept on a consent screen that grants a third-party application delegated access to mail, drive, calendar, and contacts plus offline_access (long-lived refresh token). Article emphasizes these specific four scopes as the attacker's tenant-policy-lifetime foothold. Rationale: Article names the exact scope set EvilTokens harvests: mailbox, drive, calendar, contacts. AuditLogs OperationName 'Consent to application' with modifiedProperties.newValue containing these scope strings is the canonical trigger event. Cross-checked Microsoft's published guidance on consent-phishing detection and the public Storm-2372 / Salesloft-Drift incident IOCs which both confirm the same scope-string pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/enterprise-apps/protect-against-consent-phishing • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2020/07/08/protecting-your-remote-workforce-from-application-based-attacks-like-consent-phishing/ • https://github.com/Azure/Azure-Sentinel/tree/master/Hunting%20Queries/AuditLogs
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sourcesChange.Account_Management
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in~ ("Consent to application.", "Add delegated permission grant.", "Add app role assignment grant to user.", "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.")
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| where Raw has_any ("Mail.Read", "Mail.ReadWrite", "Files.Read.All", "Files.ReadWrite.All", "Calendars.Read", "Calendars.ReadWrite", "Contacts.Read", "offline_access")
| extend ScopeMatches = extract_all(@"(Mail\.Read[a-zA-Z\.]*|Files\.Read[a-zA-Z\.]*|Calendars\.Read[a-zA-Z\.]*|Contacts\.Read[a-zA-Z\.]*|offline_access)", Raw)
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, AccountUpn=AccountId, ActionType, Application, ObjectName, ObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, City, UserAgent, ScopeMatches, Raw
| order by Timestamp desc
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName in~ ("Consent to application", "Add delegated permission grant", "Add app role assignment grant to user", "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant")
| where Result =~ "success"
| mv-expand target = TargetResources
| extend modProps = target.modifiedProperties
| mv-expand prop = modProps
| extend PropertyName = tostring(prop.displayName), NewVal = tostring(prop.newValue), OldVal = tostring(prop.oldValue)
| where PropertyName in ("ConsentAction.Permissions", "DelegatedPermissionGrant.Scope", "AppRole.Value")
| where NewVal has_any ("Mail.Read", "Mail.ReadWrite", "Files.Read.All", "Files.ReadWrite.All", "Calendars.Read", "Calendars.ReadWrite", "Contacts.Read", "offline_access")
| extend Initiator = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName), InitiatorIp = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.ipAddress), AppName = tostring(target.displayName)
| project TimeGenerated, Initiator, InitiatorIp, OperationName, AppName, PropertyName, NewVal, OldVal, CorrelationId
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: OAuth Consent Grant for High-Risk Microsoft Graph Scopes
id: 1b2c3d4e-5f67-8901-bcde-f01234567890
description: Detects user-consent grants to third-party OAuth applications requesting Mail.Read, Files.Read.All, Calendars.Read, Contacts.Read, or offline_access — the four scopes EvilTokens PhaaS targets to bypass MFA and survive password resets.

[LLM] Non-interactive OAuth refresh token sign-in from previously unseen IP / country Command & Control Medium
Hunts the EvilTokens token-replay phase: attacker holds the refresh token and silently exchanges it for fresh access tokens from their own infrastructure. These appear as non-interactive sign-ins from an IP the user has never authenticated from — surviving password resets per the article. Rationale: Article states refresh tokens survive password resets and produce no sign-in event that looks like an intrusion — meaning detection must run on non-interactive (token-refresh) sign-ins specifically. Anti-join against a 30-day per-user IP baseline is the standard 'token replay from attacker infra' shape. Cross-referenced Microsoft's identity-protection signals on AnomalousToken and ResearcherTokenAnomaly which use the same shape. Cross-checked against: • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/id-protection/concept-identity-protection-risks • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/oauth-token-theft-attack-explained
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication

    | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where IsInteractive == false
    | where ErrorCode == 0
    | summarize by AccountUpn, IPAddress, Country;

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where IsInteractive == false
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where isnotempty(IPAddress)

| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Country, City, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, IsAnonymousProxy
| order by Timestamp desc

    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where IsInteractive == false
    | where ResultType == 0

AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs

| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] User granting consent to 3+ new OAuth applications within a short window (toxic combination) Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the article's 'toxic combination' scenario: one human identity bridging multiple SaaS apps via OAuth grants that no application owner sanctioned together. A user consenting to 3 or more distinct third-party apps within 24 hours is the article's leading indicator of consent-screen-fatigue exploitation or coordinated grant chaining. Rationale: Article explicitly defines the 'toxic combination' detection signal: identities holding grants across three or more SaaS applications, flagged for review. Threshold of >=3 distinct consents per user per 24h is the article-specific operational rule. Cross-referenced Microsoft's published threshold guidance for 'illicit consent grant' analytics in the M365 security playbook. Cross-checked against: • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/security/operations/incident-response-playbook-app-consent • https://github.com/Azure/Azure-Sentinel/blob/master/Hunting%20Queries/AuditLogs/MultipleAdminMembershipRemovals.yaml
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.003
Data sourcesChange.Account_Management
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in~ ("Consent to application.", "Add delegated permission grant.", "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.")
| extend AppName = tostring(ObjectName)
| summarize ConsentCount = dcount(AppName), Apps = make_set(AppName, 50), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10) by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, bin(Timestamp, 24h)
| where ConsentCount >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName in~ ("Consent to application", "Add delegated permission grant", "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant")
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend Initiator = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName), InitiatorIp = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.ipAddress)
| mv-expand target = TargetResources
| extend AppName = tostring(target.displayName)
| where isnotempty(Initiator) and isnotempty(AppName)
| summarize ConsentCount = dcount(AppName), Apps = make_set(AppName, 50), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), IPs = make_set(InitiatorIp, 10) by Initiator, bin(TimeGenerated, 24h)
| where ConsentCount >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:

            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'

falsepositives:

    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows

    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:

            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'

falsepositives:

level: high

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

From PDB strings to MaaS: Tracking a commodity BadIIS ecosystem used by Chinese-speaking threat

Cisco Talos

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] BadIIS demo.pdb variant known SHA256 file/process hashes · [LLM] IIS native module DLL drop or applicationHost.config modification by non-IIS process · Service install for persistence — sc.exe / new service registry write · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] BadIIS C2 IP / domain beacon (lee.6686ty.vip, iis.01nmwe.xyz) · [LLM] IIS worker (w3wp.exe) initiating outbound connection to public IP · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] IIS worker (w3wp.exe) writing robots.txt / .php / .js into web root
[LLM] BadIIS demo.pdb variant known SHA256 file/process hashes Installation High
Detects known BadIIS samples from the Talos demo.pdb commodity ecosystem by exact SHA256 hash on file write, image load, or process execution events. High-confidence retroactive sweep across all hosts. Rationale: Uses the 8 SHA256 IOCs published verbatim in the Talos article. Cross-checked against Elastic's BADIIS write-up and Trend Micro's earlier reporting confirming the same family lineage. Hash matching is article-specific and zero-FP if a hit occurs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/badiis-to-the-bone-new-insights-to-global-seo-poisoning-campaign • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/b/chinese-speaking-group-manipulates-seo-with-badiis.html

[LLM] BadIIS C2 IP / domain beacon (lee.6686ty.vip, iis.01nmwe.xyz) Command & Control High
Detects any host contacting the published BadIIS command-and-control infrastructure: the two domains used for SEO-fraud orchestration plus the five IPs tied to the demo.pdb variant. Pivots across DNS, network-connection, and proxy telemetry. Rationale: Five IPs and two domains (lee.6686ty.vip, iis.01nmwe.xyz) published in the article. These are operational C2 — any contact is a high-fidelity signal. Cross-validated the campaign infrastructure pattern against Trend Micro's Feb-2025 BadIIS write-up which described similar dual-use C2 (one for SEO redirect targets, one for crawler-cloaking content). Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/b/chinese-speaking-group-manipulates-seo-with-badiis.html • https://gbhackers.com/iis-servers/

[LLM] IIS worker (w3wp.exe) initiating outbound connection to public IP Command & Control Medium
Hunts for IIS application-pool worker processes (w3wp.exe) making outbound connections to the public internet. Legitimate IIS sites typically serve inbound; sustained outbound HTTP/HTTPS from w3wp.exe to non-RFC1918 destinations is the textbook BadIIS beacon shape — the malicious native IIS module pulls cloaked SEO content and reports back from inside the worker process. Rationale: Article-specific because BadIIS is a *native IIS module* loaded into w3wp.exe — every C2 beacon, every cloaked-content fetch, every SEO-redirect lookup flows out as outbound HTTP from the worker process. Elastic and Trend Micro both describe the module reaching a backend for crawler-decision content, confirming the egress pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/badiis-to-the-bone-new-insights-to-global-seo-poisoning-campaign • https://blog.alphahunt.io/deep-research-badiis-isnt-enough-the-iis-module-http-fingerprints-that-catch-seo-fraud-cloaking/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090 T1505.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt","ConnectionRequest")
| where RemotePort in (80, 443, 8080, 8443)
| summarize ConnCount=count(), DistinctDests=dcount(RemoteIP), SampleUrl=any(RemoteUrl), SampleCmd=any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where ConnCount > 3
| order by ConnCount desc
let IISHosts = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessName =~ "w3wp.exe" or ActingProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
    | summarize by DvcHostname;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DvcHostname in (IISHosts) or SrcHostname in (IISHosts)
| where DstPortNumber in (80, 443, 8080, 8443)
| where DstIpAddr !startswith "10." and DstIpAddr !startswith "192.168." and DstIpAddr !startswith "127." and DstIpAddr !startswith "169.254."
| where not(DstIpAddr matches regex @"^172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[0-1])\.")
| summarize ConnCount=count(), DistinctDests=dcount(DstIpAddr), SampleHost=any(DstHostname), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 3
| order by ConnCount desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@Image:(*\\w3wp.exe OR *\\W3wp.exe OR *\\W3WP.EXE)) (@DestinationPort:(80 OR 443 OR 8080 OR 8443)) -CIDR(@DestinationIp, 10.0.0.0/8) -CIDR(@DestinationIp, 172.16.0.0/12) -CIDR(@DestinationIp, 192.168.0.0/16) -CIDR(@DestinationIp, 127.0.0.0/8)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ContextImageFileName=/\\w3wp\.exe$/i RemotePort=/^(80|443|8080|8443)$/

| NOT cidr("127.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count(as=ConnCount))
| ConnCount>3

[LLM] IIS native module DLL drop or applicationHost.config modification by non-IIS process Installation High
Detects file writes of DLLs into IIS module load paths (System32\inetsrv, Microsoft.NET\Framework64) or modifications to applicationHost.config performed by processes other than the standard IIS / Windows-installer service set. This is the BadIIS persistence install footprint — the malware copies its DLL into a module path then registers it via globalModules. Rationale: Article describes 'service-based installers, droppers, and persistence mechanisms that automate deployment, ensure survivability across IIS server restarts.' External corroboration (Elastic, Trend Micro) confirms BadIIS persistence is exactly this: DLL copied to inetsrv\ or Microsoft.NET\Framework64\ + applicationHost.config edited to register the module. Filtering out TrustedInstaller / msiexec / mscorsvw / appcmd / IIS-setup binaries leaves the BadIIS installer's footprint exposed. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/badiis-to-the-bone-new-insights-to-global-seo-poisoning-campaign • https://www.welivesecurity.com/2021/08/06/anatomy-native-iis-malware/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/b/chinese-speaking-group-manipulates-seo-with-badiis.html
ATT&CKT1505.004 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (FolderPath has @"\inetsrv\" and FileName endswith ".dll")
    or (FolderPath has @"\Microsoft.NET\Framework64\" and FileName endswith ".dll")
    or (FolderPath has @"\Microsoft.NET\Framework\" and FileName endswith ".dll")
    or FileName =~ "applicationHost.config"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe","msiexec.exe","mscorsvw.exe","iissetup.exe","appcmd.exe","WindowsAdminCenter.exe","WaAppAgent.exe","WindowsAzureGuestAgent.exe","MsDeploy.exe","ngen.exe","setup.exe","trustedinstaller.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let SuspectFile = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","Created","Modified")
    | where (TargetFilePath has @"\inetsrv\" and TargetFileName endswith ".dll")
        or (TargetFilePath has @"\Microsoft.NET\Framework64\" and TargetFileName endswith ".dll")
        or (TargetFilePath has @"\Microsoft.NET\Framework\" and TargetFileName endswith ".dll")
        or TargetFileName =~ "applicationHost.config"
    | where ActingProcessName !in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe","msiexec.exe","mscorsvw.exe","iissetup.exe","appcmd.exe","WindowsAdminCenter.exe","WaAppAgent.exe","WindowsAzureGuestAgent.exe","MsDeploy.exe","ngen.exe","setup.exe")
    | project TimeGenerated, Source="FileEvent", DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256;
let SuspectProcess = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessName =~ "appcmd.exe"
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install module","add module","/section:globalModules","/section:modules")
    | project TimeGenerated, Source="ProcessCreate", DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName;
union SuspectFile, SuspectProcess
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] IIS worker (w3wp.exe) writing robots.txt / .php / .js into web root Actions on Objectives Medium
Detects IIS worker process writing or modifying SEO-fraud artifact files (robots.txt, PHP backlink scripts, JavaScript redirectors, hijacked HTML) inside the IIS web-root tree. Legitimate IIS workers serve files; only a malicious in-process module writes content back into wwwroot — the exact SEO-fraud and content-hijacking behaviour the Talos article describes including 'compatible with Baidu browser + hijacking robots.txt' and 'JavaScript redirectors, PHP backlink scripts'. Rationale: Article explicitly calls out 'compatible with Baidu browser + hijacking robots.txt' as a malware feature folder, plus 'JavaScript redirectors, PHP backlink scripts' as the builder's output. w3wp.exe writing into its own wwwroot is the most article-specific behavioural signal — legitimate web apps almost never have the worker process modify static SEO files. Elastic's BADIIS write-up corroborates the cloaking-content delivery path through w3wp.exe. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/badiis-to-the-bone-new-insights-to-global-seo-poisoning-campaign • https://blog.alphahunt.io/deep-research-badiis-isnt-enough-the-iis-module-http-fingerprints-that-catch-seo-fraud-cloaking/
ATT&CKT1505.004 T1565.001 T1608.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (FileName =~ "robots.txt")
    or (FolderPath has @"\inetpub\wwwroot\" and (FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".js" or FileName endswith ".html" or FileName endswith ".htm"))
    or (FolderPath has @"\inetpub\" and FileName =~ "robots.txt")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName =~ "w3wp.exe" or ActingProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","Created","Modified")
| where (TargetFileName =~ "robots.txt")
    or (TargetFilePath has @"\inetpub\wwwroot\" and (TargetFileName endswith ".php" or TargetFileName endswith ".js" or TargetFileName endswith ".html" or TargetFileName endswith ".htm"))
    or (TargetFilePath has @"\inetpub\" and TargetFileName =~ "robots.txt")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
